query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A partial substitution of Mo with Nb in the equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy will maintain high yield strength while enhancing room-temperature plasticity.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy exhibiting a compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; the high Mo content increases the overall electronegativity difference, which correlates with reduced plasticity.
generation.intervention: Replace a fraction of Mo with Nb (e.g., modify the composition to NbZrTiHf(Mo_xNb_1-x) with x less than 1), thereby increasing the Nb/Mo ratio while keeping other elemental ratios unaltered.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed to retain its disordered BCC phase and is tested for compressive properties at room temperature. The substitution should be done within limits that preserve the solid solution strengthening provided by Mo.
generation.structural_mediator: The balance of lattice distortion in the BCC matrix; substituting some Mo with Nb is expected to reduce the overall electronegativity difference without disrupting the single-phase BCC structure.
generation.mechanism: High Mo content contributes to a larger electronegativity difference, which intensifies lattice distortion and hinders dislocation motion, thereby reducing plasticity. By partially replacing Mo with Nb, which has been shown to improve fracture strain with only a modest effect on yield strength, the alloy should experience a more favorable balance between dislocation mobility and solution strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit similar high compressive yield strength (around 1700 MPa) while displaying significantly improved plasticity (i.e., higher compressive strain before fracture) compared to the original composition.
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy has a compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa but suffers from limited plasticity due to high Mo-induced electronegativity differences.
generation.boundary: The substitution must be limited so that the Mo content remains sufficient to provide the necessary solid solution strengthening; excessive Nb substitution may lead to a drop in strength or the formation of unwanted secondary phases.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Nb/Mo ratio for maximum ductility improvement without strength compromise is not precisely known; experimental tuning will be required to determine the best balance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of alloys with gradually increasing Nb content at the expense of Mo (e.g., varying the Mo_xNb_1-x ratio, where x decreases from 1 toward a lower bound) while keeping the other elements equiatomic. Process the alloys under identical conditions to ensure retention of the disordered BCC phase and measure their room-temperature compressive mechanical properties.
measurements: Microstructural phase analysis via XRD or TEM
Assessment of electronegativity difference changes via compositional analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the partial substitution of Mo with Nb results in either a significant reduction in compressive yield strength, the formation of undesired phases, or no improvement (or even a deterioration) in compressive ductility compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention.
